title: CoreWeave Is Accelerating To Escape Velocity Thanks To GPU Shortages
author: Timothy Prickett Morgan
text:
CLOUD

CoreWeave Is Accelerating To Escape Velocity Thanks To GPU Shortages

Timothy Prickett Morgan

Timothy Prickett
Morgan

Co-Editor, Co-Founder, The Next Platform

Published
thu 12 Nov 2026 // 00:50 UTC

CoreWeave, arguably the king of the neoclouds that focus exclusively on AI processing as opposed to the full breadth of compute in the datacenter, has had its share of doubters and critics. And the consequent whipsawing around of its share price and people go bull or bear on it.But thanks to the undersupply of GPUs in the world and the extreme desire to use them to train AI models and to run inference workloads against them, pricing for the vintage GPUs in the CoreWeave fleet are going up and up and up, and that means the company’s revenues are also rising and, not at all coincidentally but quite deliberately, so is CoreWeave’s operating profits. Which is all well and good. But the heavy debt load that CoreWeave has – roughly $48 billion by our math – is very expensive to service.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

But here is the thing. That debt is being used to fund capital expenses that expand the CoreWeave datacenter footprint and its AI server fleet, and the quicker it builds out this fleet, the quicker it can start booking revenue against it. Companies are prepaying billions of dollars for capacity ahead of time, which is now being used to fund capex as well, and an even larger increase in demand for GPUs or a crimping of supply would only help CoreWeave make more money sooner.In short, the economics of the GenAI boom are starting to play in CoreWeave’s favor, which company co-founder and chief executive officer Michael Intrator explained as part of his going over the company’s financial results for the third quarter of 2026.“In July, we increased pricing across SKUs by approximately 25 percent, followed by another 10 percent increase later in the quarter,” Intrator explained. “Pricing has continued to move higher in Q4, more than offsetting cost increases. We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four- and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt. Long-term commitments provide the visibility that supports our build-out. Short-term contracts let us respond to a strong pricing environment and earn premium returns. We weigh that trade-off contract by contract, assessing the full economics of an investment, the revenue it can earn, the cost of operating it, and the cost of financing it. Strong demand gives us choices in how we best create durable value.”To make his point, Intrator added that rental prices for Nvidia “Ampere” A100 GPUs in the CoreWeave fleet rose by 30 percent sequentially in the third quarter, and rental prices for “Hopper” H100 and H200 GPUs rose by 50 percent sequentially. That’s pretty damned good for the A100s, which are six and a half years old (they started shipping in May 2020), and the H100s, which are four years old (they started shipping in September 2022). The A100s have been written down completely is my guess and the H100s are probably going to be written down entirely next year. This means selling their capacity is very profitable even after taking out operating costs for the systems that use these vintage GPUs.

To further make his point, Intrator said that 130,000 GPUs would come off contract and be open for new deals at higher prices, and another 170,000 GPUs would be up for renewal in 2028. (My guess is that CoreWeave has around 1.25 million GPUs installed right now, based on its active power, just to give you a sense of how small a part of the fleet the renewals in 2027 and 2028 represent.) Intrator did a little math and said that the 2027 renewals would generate $4 billion in incremental annualized revenues at the current (and higher) prices and this would grow to an incremental $10 billion annualized revenues for the 2028 renewals.“If datacenter construction across the sector were to slow, installed compute becomes scarcer and the knock-on effect is that GPU pricing may stay higher for longer,” Intrator explained. “In that scenario, being first matters. Our installed base comes off contract, fully paid, years ahead of most others in the market. We're well positioned across a range of market conditions. If the industry builds quickly, we grow with it. If supply is delayed, our installed paid-off fleet becomes more valuable. We do not build our plan on that scenario. The plan rests on contracted demand, success-based capex and the contracts we are already signing.”All of this is why the chart below makes sense:

There is a direct correlation to the size of the CoreWeave GPU fleet, which I have estimated based on the active power each quarter, and the revenue backlog that CoreWeave is able to build. The correlation is very strong, as you can see. And it makes perfect sense.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

But like a shark, the business has to keep moving to keep building that backlog, and at some point the debt load has to stop growing faster than revenues. That has to happen before the GenAI bubble bursts. I still believe that it will be very hard to find the power for the buildout that is expected in the IT sector in 2029 and 2030. We seem to be relatively safe in 2027 and into 2028, given so much of the capacity purchased is prepaid.

In the third quarter ended in September, CoreWeave booked $3.66 billion in sales, up 2.7X year on year and up 42.2 percent sequentially from the second quarter. Operating income was actually a positive $207 million, compared to an operating income of $52 million a year ago. But because of the debt service, the company’s net loss expanded by a factor of 6.4X to $709 million. Hence, losses are outpacing revenue growth. Not taking on more debt and using the proceeds from price increases to fund capex expansion – which is indeed the plan – will help get things back into whack. Or more precisely, into whack for the first time in CoreWeave’s history.We shall see. But, the price increases and the demand to support them are encouraging signs.If you like to drill down into the numbers yourself, here are the trends since Q1 2024:

CoreWeave exited the quarter with just under $5.6 billion in cash and equivalents and shelled out $14.5 billion for capital expenses. For the year so far, CoreWeave has spent $30.7 billion on datacenter gear and facilities. The company ended the quarter with a revenue backlog of $132.5 billion, up 2.4X year on year.
